chunks: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd narrated from Muḥammad ibn Shuʿayb, who said:

I wrote to him that a man proposed to his paternal uncle for his daughter. So he instructed one of his brothers to marry his daughter—the one he had proposed for—to him. The man then erred in the name of the young woman, though her name was Fāṭimah, and he called her by a name other than her own; and the man had no daughter with the name mentioned by the one conducting the marriage.
So he (عليه السلام) wrote back: “There is no harm in it.”

key_terms.الْجَارِيَةِ: the young woman intended in marriage
key_terms.الْمُزَوِّجُ: the one conducting the marriage contract
key_terms.فَاطِمَةَ: the actual name of the bride
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: there is no harm in it; it is unobjectionable
key_terms.يُزَوِّجَهُ: to marry him off to her in the contract

ai.seo_question: Is a marriage contract valid if the bride’s name is mistakenly mentioned incorrectly?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses a marriage contract in which the bride’s name was mentioned incorrectly, despite the intended woman being clearly identified. The Imam (عليه السلام) ruled that there was no problem with it, indicating the validity of the contract when the intended person is known and there is no real ambiguity.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: Hadith.4470 - Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hamid narrated from Muhammad ibn Shuayb who said:

I wrote to Imam (as) regarding a man who proposed marriage to his uncle's daughter.
The uncle instructed one of his brothers to marry his daughter to the man.
However, during the marriage contract, the man mistakenly mentioned a different name instead of the daughter's actual name, which was Fatimah. The man did not have any daughter by the name he mentioned during the contract.
The Imam (as) responded: "There is no harm in it."
